newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Iraq must recognise no-fly zones -Kuwait official.
newsitem.headline: Iraq must recognise no-fly zones -Kuwait official.

text.p: Kuwait appeared unsatisfied by Baghdad's decision to halt attacks against U.S. and allied warplanes policing no-fly zones over Iraq and a Kuwait official said Saddam Hussein had to recognise the zones.
The senior official said on Friday night the Iraqi leader must recognise the no-fly zones, including an expanded one in the south up to the 33rd parallel on the outskirts of Baghdad.

The Kuwaiti government has not yet officially responded to the latest Iraqi announcement that appeared aimed at defusing the current crisis with the United States, which said it was encouraged but that the situation would be closely monitored.

Baghdad's announcement came shortly after U.S. Stealth F-117A radar-evading aircraft landed in Kuwait as part of a major American military build-up in the region amid expectations of an imminent U.S. strike against Iraq.

Iraq, in a fresh standoff with Washington over the expansion of the southern no-fly zone, told Kuwait on Thursday it would be committing an act of war if it allowed the Stealth warplanes to use its territory for attacks on it.

Iraq had also shot at Western planes patrolling the no-fly zones after the United States fired cruise missiles last week against air defence targets in southern Iraq in retaliation for Iraq's military intervention in the country's north to help a Kurdish group fighting a rival Kurdish faction.
The U.S.-led force had set up the no-fly zone in the north after the 1991 Gulf War to protect Kurds from attacks by Iraqi troops.

The Kuwaiti official said that some of the 1991 Gulf War allies also demanded Iraq's "removal of air defences from the new section" between the 32nd and 33rd parallels in addition to its recognition of the zones.

He was speaking after the Iraqi News Agency (INA) quoted a spokesman for the ruling Revolutionary Command Council as saying Iraq "decided today to suspend our military reaction (until further notice) to the parallel lines" as of 2000 GMT Friday.
But the Iraqi agency said Baghdad still considered the five-year-old Western-enforced no-fly zones to be illegitimate according to international law and U.N. Security Council resolutions.
The expanded southern zone was announced last week following the U.S. cruise missiles attacks.

Washington, which had also dispatched to the region a second aircraft carrier group as well as B-52 long-range bombers to confront Iraq, said it would judge Baghdad on its actions, not its statements.

Defence Secretary William Perry will travel to the Middle East to consult with allies, U.S. Defence officials said on Friday. The officials declined to give details on when and where Perry was going, but they did not deny earlier reports that he would visit Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain and Turkey.

Prior to the Iraqi announcement the Gulf's non-Arab power Iran said it would be "quite sorry" if the United States attacked Iraq but predicted any new war would be short-lived because Iraq was unable to resist.

Western military officers in the Gulf agree. They said Iraq posed a limited threat to U.S. warships in the region with its naval forces damaged in the Gulf War despite some concern over its ability to mine northern Gulf waters.
Iran, which fought Iraq in their 1980-88 war, stayed neutral in the Gulf War although it is opposed to the presence of non-Gulf forces in the oil-rich region.
U.S. warplanes and warships are moving into position for possible raids against Iraq after Iraqi forces fired a surface- to-air missile at U.S. fighters over northern Iraq on Wednesday.
With the exception of the British, most allies have been tepid at best in their support for the U.S. missile attacks.
